title: Late-onset epilepsy and epilepsy surgery: clinical characteristics and long-term outcomes
summary: One in three people with epilepsy still have seizures despite medication – they could benefit from brain surgery. There are an increasing number of patients whose epilepsy begins after the age of 40, but we know very little about how they fare in terms of seizures and mental performance after surgery. We will therefore evaluate all cases in which patients underwent surgery after the age of 40 and examine the development of their seizure frequency and cognitive functions. We will also look at what changes in the removed brain tissue and what other factors influence the outcome. For comparison, we will use patients with early-onset epilepsy (operated on and treated with medication only) and patients with late-onset epilepsy who have received medication only. The aim is to find criteria that predict when surgery is appropriate for late-onset, drug-resistant epilepsy. This will enable doctors to better decide who can benefit from surgery.

interventions.name: Patients who underwent epilepsy surgery at our center between 2003 and 2022 and had late-onset epilepsy (over the age of 40).
Patients with early-onset epilepsy, as well as patients with early- and late-onset epilepsy who were treated with medication alone or without surgery.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients who underwent epilepsy surgery at our center (Clinic and Polyclinic for Epileptology, or Clinic and Polyclinic for Neurosurgery at the University Hospital Bonn) between 2003 and 2022 with late-onset epilepsy (over 40 years of age).
Control group: Patients with early-onset epilepsy, as well as patients with early- and late-onset epilepsy who were treated with medication only or without surgery.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients under 18 years of age or without epilepsy
